solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Disposal of waste article I found in railway halt

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so these pieces go within the stopping point

parts.note: a railway halt is a station
an is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A notice about dumping rubbish, with some article turning up at a little country station.
explanation.walkthrough: The inserted pair goes in right after the first letter of the halt, not in its middle, which is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanitation is the public service of removing sewage and refuse, so it covers the disposal of waste.

clue.text: Spear small fish

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a pike is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: An instruction to harpoon a little fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To spike something is to pierce it with a pointed object, a synonym of spear as a verb.

clue.text: A spot of dancing close with tango society?

parts.note: nigh means near or close
T is tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a club is a society of members

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a dance society might do a little dancing, finishing with a tango.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A spot of dancing' reads as 'a bit of dancing', but here spot means a place, a venue.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightclub is a venue, or spot, where people go to dance late at night.

clue.text: Banned words used to thanks and surprise

parts.note: ta is an informal British word for thanks
boo is the word shouted to surprise or startle someone

explanation.surface: Certain forbidden words are used in thanking and in expressing surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is prohibited by social custom, so it is banned in conversation or behaviour.

clue.text: That lacks worth, ultimately?

indicators.note: a word that lacks something has had that part taken out

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very last letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of worth

explanation.surface: A question about what ultimately has no worth.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove H from THAT to leave TAT; read whole, the clue also describes tat, which is cheap, worthless stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: Tat is British slang for tasteless or shoddy goods, items with no real value.

clue.text: Published mounted sketch that's superficial

parts.note: a book that is out has been published

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounted means going upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to draw is to sketch

explanation.surface: A sketch put on display and published turns out to be shallow.
explanation.definitionFit: Outward means relating only to the surface or outside appearance, which is what superficial describes.

clue.text: Waiter cries — is completely lacking one salad ingredient

indicators.note: completely lacking means every instance of the item is taken away, not just one

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A waiter complains that the salad is missing an ingredient.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip all three I's from WAITER CRIES IS and the remaining letters, in order, spell WATERCRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Watercress is a peppery leafy plant commonly eaten raw in salads.

clue.text: One in wild gang growing old

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
something wild is out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A member of an unruly gang is getting on in years.
explanation.definitionFit: Aging, the American spelling of ageing, means becoming older, the same as growing old.

clue.text: English city, but to the west, that's associated with The Wash?

parts.note: Bath is a city in Somerset, England

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means running right to left, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A geography quiz: which English city lies to the west of the Wash?
explanation.walkthrough: The Wash is a broad bay on England's east coast; here it just means a wash in the bath, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bathtub is the vessel you sit in for a wash, so it is closely linked with washing.

clue.text: Late yawn may be hidden here

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: a polite yawn is covered up at the back of your palm

explanation.surface: A late night leaves someone stifling a yawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer into two words: a yawn is hidden behind a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Behindhand is an old-fashioned word for being late or in arrears with payments or work.

clue.text: Conductor let end of Kyrie and Credo go wrong

indicators.note: letters that go wrong fall out of their proper order and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: end of picks out only the final letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the final letter of Kyrie
taken as written

explanation.surface: A choir's conductor lets the end of two parts of the Mass go badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests a musician beside the Kyrie and Credo, but it means an electrical conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: An electrode is a solid electrical conductor through which current enters or leaves a circuit.

clue.text: Relating to X marks in elite exam

parts.note: the elect are a chosen elite
an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: A top school's exam where the answers are marked with crosses.
explanation.walkthrough: X marks look like crosses on test papers; here they are the crosses voters put on ballot papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Electoral describes elections, where voters mark their choice on a ballot paper with a cross.

clue.text: Like hard wood

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A description of some timber as being like hardwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is a tree whose tough pale timber is a widely used wood.

clue.text: Marine mollusc moves quickly, shedding skin

indicators.note: shedding its skin, a word loses its outer layer: the first and last letters go

parts.note: to scuttle is to hurry with short quick steps

explanation.surface: A sea creature darts about as it moults.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuttle is short for cuttlefish, a sea mollusc related to squid and octopus.

clue.text: Acrobat that's often full of drink?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a performer who does somersaults
second meaning: a flat-bottomed drinking glass

explanation.surface: A circus performer who is frequently drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full of drink' suggests a drunken person, but the second meaning is a container that literally holds the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbler is both a gymnast performing flips and a straight-sided glass for beverages.

clue.text: Gloomy main actor — heartless, even

parts.note: the lead is the principal role in a play or film

indicators.note: heartless removes the centre of the word, so only its outside letters remain

parts.note: the outside letters of even

explanation.surface: A star performer described as morose, even heartless.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaden skies or moods are dull, heavy and grey, a figurative synonym for gloomy.

clue.text: Tree covered in tinsel mainly

indicators.note: covered in means held inside the following words, enclosed by their letters

parts.note: the letters run across the boundary of the two words

explanation.surface: A Christmas tree draped mostly in tinsel.
explanation.definitionFit: The elm is a tall deciduous tree common in British hedgerows and parks.

clue.text: Strong wind meeting hill church. This could strip surface

parts.note: a blow is a gale
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A gale batters a hilltop church, enough to strip its walls.
explanation.definitionFit: A blowtorch's hot flame is used to burn off old paint, stripping a surface back.

clue.text: Relating to vision of paradise that is created initially

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: the first letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A description of a vision of paradise when it was first made.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic is an adjective meaning concerning the eye or sight, so it relates to vision.

clue.text: Expression of surprise after strange card game

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
my! is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone gasps after a peculiar game of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the exclamation behind the word for strange, though it comes first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rummy is a card game in which players collect sets and sequences of cards.

clue.text: Very good and lawful petition

parts.note: so means very, as in so kind
licit means permitted, proper and lawful

explanation.surface: A petition that is perfectly proper and legal.
explanation.definitionFit: To solicit is to ask earnestly for something, so it works as the verb petition.

clue.text: Have the ability to dance — but not the repeat

indicators.note: dropping the repeat means the doubled half of the word is removed

parts.note: the cancan is a high-kicking dance

explanation.surface: A dancer is able to perform, as long as there is no encore.
explanation.definitionFit: Can is the modal verb expressing being able to do something.

clue.text: Right country for ancient Italian

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
Oman is a country in Arabia

explanation.surface: Choosing the correct nation to suit an old Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman was a citizen of ancient Rome, the classical Italian city and empire.

clue.text: Common metal I label unknown, rather sarcastically

parts.note: iron is a common metal
taken as written
to call something is to label or name it
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Someone calls iron an unknown metal, with heavy sarcasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironically means saying the opposite of what is meant, close in sense to somewhat sarcastically.
